CONSECRATION OF THE COLONIAL BISHOPS. On Wednesday, (St. Bartholomew's Day) Aug. 34th, the consecration of the five newly elected Colonial Bishops took place in Westminster Abbey. Jri consequence of the indisposition of his Grace the Archbishop of Canterbury, the ceremony was performed by the Bishops of London, Winchester, Rochester, and Chichester. þÿ The usual plovers of the Church having been read, the lit. Rev. Dr. Coleridge, late Bishop of Barbadoes, preached the sermon, selecting for his text the 4.3rd chapter of Isaiah, 5ih and 6th verses. The Right Rev. Prelate spoke ai some length on the universality of the Redeemer's kingdom ; he showed that, in the prophesies, it was clearly developed, and in the law it self not obscurely intimated. In adverting to the high position our country Holds amongst the kingdoms of the earth, he remarked ihat wc boast, and not without justice, of our preeminence ; hut it ought to be recollected that our moral and intellectual gieatness, our na val and military renown, the spiead of our commerce and the abundance of our weaiih, were not given us for worldly purposes alone, but as instruim nts wherewith to work for the glory of Cod, and what could be more wor thy of such a country than the co-ex tension, with its influence of the gospel which the Sa viour came to deliver. The Bishop next alluded to the high solemnity of the day. Never, he believed, were the principles of the Augtican Church more thoroughly silted, or better understood, than during the temporary cloud that passed over the Chinch during the

seventeenth century. Though dead, the venerable prelates and clergy of that day speak to us in their deathless wi ittngs. True to her apostolical origin and primitive purity, the Church which they loved and for which they would have laid down their lives, has risen with the exicge cies of the times It is no longer satisfied with the scanty provision tor its distant members or for the conversion of the heathen. It is now, so to speak, putting forth off shoots from the I'urent Church, and sending forth prelate after pieinte to the remotest portion ot her spii itual jurisdiction. It was necessary she should arouse herself As an affectionate parent she sought Iter childieu, who are an integral part of herself, on whose safety depends in a great measure tier own. Translations of the Bible and Liturgy have been made into various languages, but this should not be all. Ministers must be sent forth to expound them, for without efficient pastors the spiritual interests of a people can never be duly consulted. In almost all our colonies there have been some clergymen, but there has been no presiding and cuntroling power. In some cases, indeed, success has attended the efforts of the clergy, bui this has been the success of individuals not of the system There has been no voice of authority to defend the clergy þÿ no counsellor for them in their þÿdifficulties no one into w hose bosom they might pour their private difficulties, theit pastoral trials, their personal dangers There w as no chief minister to cement the clergy

into one influential body þÿ to promote ' the unity spirit of in the bond of peace." There w as no one to confirm the voting, to send additional clergymen and under such circumstances it was impossible to hope for arty measure of success. þÿ The prelate concluded

1 his sermon by an eloquent appeal to the newly elected Bishops. He warned them of the many difficulties they must encounter in the discharge of their high and holy duties He trusted they would assert the Apostolical character of the Church, and maintain her Catholicity þÿ imbibe her scriptural principles, and prepare the way for a stricter discipline, and enjoin uniformity as far as practicable; that they would be firm, yet tempeiing it with mildness, cautious without timidity ; that they would be examples of their own injunctions, and cherish souls through love for the Redeemer, and, as he died for all, so they would labour for all. Many a prayer would he offered up for a blessing on their labours; many a heart would wait on their progress, and they would he cheered by the promise held out to all faithful ministers that Cod would be with them, " even unto the end of the world" þÿ At the conclusion of the sermon, the Bishops elect, vested in their rochets, were presented to the Bishops acting for the Primate, by the Bishop of Chichester and Dr. Coleridge. The Queen's mandate was read, and the usual oaths administered. All questions having been answered the Bishops elect put on the rest of the episcopal habit, and received the imposition of hands þÿ "he holy communion was adininistcied to a large portion of the congregation, at the close of the service.

We make little doubt but that the question of the t ight of search, which Great Britain has asserted to he the only means of suppressing the slave-trade on the coast of Africa, will ultimately lead to a maritime war It is in vain that our government has laboured incessantly to procure reciprocal treaties from al! the nations of Europe, and even from the United States of America and the Braziis, pledging them bv united public efforts to extinguish this traffic, and to submit to the right of search, mutually, a!! of their vessels trading within certain latitudes ol the coast of Africa. We have not found much difficulty in procuring these treaties from the respective states; the difficulty has not rested in the mere national contract, but in the faithful observance of its at tides. Spain, Portugal, Russia, Prussia, and even France, have entered into treaties on this subject, and, with the exception of France, til! the covenanting powers are willing Jo abide by the terms of existing tieaties, or to renew them when their present tieaties shall expire. France, as is well known, refuses to enter into auv new treaty on the subject, notwithstanding that M. Guizot during tlie last year actually made a treaty with Great Britain expressly for renewing the right of search. It is well known how much aerirnonv fie tween the two countries this question has excited þÿ it is now filling the tongue of the French press with virulence and bitterness unheard of before; and as the United .States

have positively refused to submit to a right ol search for this pm pose, it. is reasonable to suppose that the two countries, I t unee and Worth America, will be united on tins ground ol opposition to the claims ol Gieal Biil.un þÿ We cannot therefore but fotesee that tiie time will arrive, when the question of tbe right of search, and the resolute exercise of it by Great Britain, as the only effectual means of preventing the slave-trade, will lead to a war between England and Fiance.

From the New i ork Journal of Commerce, January 14, 1843. From an American residing in a foreign country, we have received the following communication : " There appears to he but one opinion abroad, that is in all countries having commercial intercourse with the United IStatcs (except China.) that this Tariff will prove ruinous not only to their trade with the U. States but will also be exceedingly prejudicial to the States themselves. It is universally admitted that the latter were never, since the formation ol the Constitution, in a worse or more embarrassed condition than they are now, both in regard to public and private credit. How can a nation so situated, afford to pay higher prices for Joreign articles? Who can afford to consume foreign broadcloths, or silks, or spirits, or various manufactured goods of cotton, &c. at the rates they must pay for them under the new Taiiff?

The trade with England, France, Holland Russia, Sweden, Spain and Portugal, will greatly suffer undct this Tariff, not to mention the West Indies, in the articles of Sugar aud Rum If the object of the high dotyparty is to diminish the consumption of Spirits, why not put 50 cents per gallon excise duty upon domestic spirits? Do they think that with whiskey at 20 a 25 cents per gallon, the consumption will he much diminished? The piesent Tariff cannot increase the revenue þÿ for those articles from which revenue is expected, are so heavily taxed in it as to amount to prohibition þÿ What commission merchant will now receive foreign consignments and be obliged to pay down such exorbitant cash duties? and what foreign merchant will be so crazy as to ship such goo to is the United States? Truly their net proceeds would he trifling indeed. What American merchant will order out goods under this Tariff ? A Chinese, system will prevail in the U States, equal to Mr- Jefferson's blessed commercial restrictions' long embargo, &c. when "we cut ofl our noses to spite our faces.1' 1 hope and trust the Congress now in session wili immediately alter their bill of last session, and make it conform to Mr. Simmons' bill Exorbitant duties are contrary to our free institutions, leading to arbitraty and tvranical measures at the custom houses' struggling and seizures. Duties should be moderate, unless we consider it desirable to adorn our nation with a Rirmingbam and a Manchester, and with their starving misera-

ble population ; we. who have such an immense eoiintrt yet uncultivated, that even the Disputed Tettilory a/fine might have supported I ('0,000 inhabitants. What shall we say then of the great extent of our Western domains? Uur rich manufacturing capitalists need not. contribute , under this Tariff, a dollar to the Central Government, for titev can consume their own wrought goods, at the people's expense, and as for tea and coffee, 1 presume they are left free of duty, for their own use. Exorbitant unties (or prohibition) have a most unchristian effect; they prevent that free intercourse between nations so necessary to make them friendly to each otner, and they tend to diminish the spread of civil and religions liberty, by impeding that intercourse which Americans should always be anxious

B&STS& TttS3NU!B33H& to promote and extend. And besides, is there nothing to apprehend from the feelings of aversion which such prohibitory duties are apt to engender towards us, among Ibreign powers? Cannot they retaliate by putting higher duties on our cotton and othe s tples? Has not England lately relaxed in her Tat iff, particularly in the articles ol provisions ? and is she not the customer for J of our great staple ? Twenty per cent on the lair value in the U. States, is as high protection as any interest should have the assutaoce to ask. On such bulky and necessary articles as salt and coal, there should be no duty. The expences of transportation across the ocean, being piotoction sufficient." By the Editors. þÿ Mr. Simmons bill does not assess the duty on the " lair value" of the article, but on the " deemed and taken" value in many instances, by which bis go per cent , becomes 30, 40, or any other per cent, which he pleases to have it.

INDIA, AFGHANISTAN, AND CHINA. The Indian mail to the 1st of December has arrived, and we have letters and papers to that date. The intelligence which they communicate, although not of an exciting na ture, is still highly interesting, in particular as tending to develope the policy about to be adopted, not only in relation to the Aflghans of Cabul, but also in regard to the inhabitants ol the districts bordering on the river Indus, and even towards the Sikhs in the Punjaub The return of all the Driiish troops through the hostile defiles of the Khyber was fully concluded ou the 7th of November. The first division, under General Pollock, succeeded in effecting their march without much difficulty. The second, commanded by General M'Caskill, was not equally fortunate, in consequence, as report states, of the neglect of crowning the heights over a most dangerous part of the defile. The plunder-loving mountaineers were on the watch, and, finding this division embarrassed in its movements near Ali Musjid, during the night of the 3d made an attack on the baggage, a considerable quantity of which is said to have fallen into tfieir hands. During the skirmishing two officers, Lieut. Christie, of the Artillery, and Ensign Nicholson, of the 30th Bengal Native Infantry, were killed, as well as upwards of 100 Sepoys killed and wounded, besides a number of camp followers. Two cannon were also taken by them, but one of the guns was retaken on the following morning as well as the carriage of the other, the Khyberries having found means of conceal-

ing the gun itself. 1 his gun was, however" subsequently destroyed by Captain Thomas and the irregulars under his orders, who formed the rear guard. With this exception, nothing of consequence appears to have occurred in the return of the troops from Jellalabad to Peshawur through the most difficult defiles in Asia. It appears we have 18 going line of-battle-ships, being seven less than last " vear ; 32 frigates, T » being o five less than last year ; 39 sloops, one less ; 39 smaller vessels, 19 less than last year; 64 steamers, four additional; 21 surveying vessels; 10 troopships; and 10 receiving ships. The line of French mail packets, to cross the Atlantic, will, it is expected, commence running next June. The packets will he 14 in number ; they are built to carry 40 guns each, and will belong to the French government. The port selected for the packet station is Cherbourg. Four of the steamers will run to and from New York ; and the rest will convey mails and passengers to and from France and the West Indies, Uracils, and the Gulf of Mexico. The whole of the postage paid to the English government for the correspondence between France and the Southern United States and the French West Indies will he lost to this country after the French Atlantic steamers have commenced running.

Isthmus op Panama Canal. The commission authorised bv the government of New Grenada to construct a canal between the two seas have concluded their survey |of the land which the canal wdl intersect, and have reported iavoorably. The chant of the Cordilleras does not extend, as had been imagined, across the isthmus. The explorers have, on the contrary, discovered a vallev very favourable for the poroses of the undertaking. The natural disposition of the waters is also favourable. The rivers, portions of the beds of which are navigable, will be made to form part of the canal. The necessary cutting will not he more than twelve miles and a half. The fall, or inclination, will be regulated hv two large locks. The entire length of this canal will be 49 miles; the breadth at the surface of the water 135 feet, and 55 at the bottom. The depth will he 20 feet, which will enable it to bo navigated by ships of from 1000 to 1 100 tons burthen 1 he cost of its completion, according to the estimate of M. Morel, the French engineer, will he 14.000,000 of francs, or 590,000/. sterling.

St Thomas, February 13, 1843. This morning a French Schooner came in consigned to us. The news site brings is that the City of þÿ Pointe a þÿPetre (Guadaloupe) is entirely devastated, att J not one single build ing left standing in it. It is supposed that 6000 people have disappeared, some how or other no one can tell, and the bodies of 4000. which began to decompose and smell offensive, were dug out of the ruins by the sailors in the Harbor and taken out to sea in boats as fast as they could, and thus get rid of them to prevent a pestilence. Out of 800 fine soldiers composing the Regiment, quartered at P. a Petie only 40 remained to tell the tale of woe ! The massy Fortifications, the Guns, the Barracks and all therein being crumbled into dust, while the mouth of the Harbor which before the event was capable of admitting ships of the heaviest burthen, became completely choked up and fotever rendered impassable by rocks being forced up from the bottom of the sea. The vessels which were at the time in port will, it is Seared never be got out, among them many large snips from France, and other vessels from America &.c. The survivors were reduced to such an awful extremity for food that whole cart-loads of (Janes were ordered in from the Country for them, and in the way to the town they rushed out and by main force intercepted the carts, and seized the Canes as if mad from hunger!! An order came down for 1000 barrels of Flour, þÿ g00 barrels P>eef, 50 trs. llice, 30 casks Fish. &o. all of which have been

procured and suit to-night by the aforesaid French Schooner and our þÿ þÿRomp. In St. Harts the Church and several massy buildings were thrown down and the earth opened in the centre of a street, for the space of 600 yards þÿ one foot wide ! In Antigua almost every building in St. Johns was thrown down including S churches while strange to say only 10 lives were lost there. Fehr. 14th 1813. The Sugar-Mills, and works either totally destroyed or so injured as to arrest the progress of the crop which some estates had just begun, and render it uncertain when the remainder can proceed with theirs. The new villages built and settled by the labourers as well as the houses on the plantations are almost all level with the ground. þÿ Falmouth Church is level with the ground as also All Saints, Lebanon at Sea view nearly so, the town of Falmouth a heap of ruins, English Harbour the same, the Dock Yard the same þÿ there, the ground sunk in many places to a great extent. The Barracks in the Kidge uninhabitable, the men put under canvas. The Engineer quarter, Commissariat and Barrack Master's the only buildings escaped damage, being of wood þÿ Dow's Hill house uninhabitable the interior having fallen completely to pieces. The Governor and family came in to town Inst night to take up their residence. On his Excellency's arrival in town, the Magistrates, Merchants and principal inhabitants who had been pieviously summoned, assembled at Government House where measures were resol ved upon for the securitv of þÿproperly. Special Gonstables sworn in. and a detachment of the 47th lieig't. marched down to the i'olice quarters to assist in case of necessity. We hear that his Excellency has lost to a large amount in Furniture, Cbinaware and Paintings &c. It is with deep concern we add that several lives have been lo.-t and many persons wound-

ed by the falling of the walls. Other Churches and Chapels iu the several parishes, have entirely fallen, or are left in a shattered condition. During the convulsiou the sea encroached considerably on the land. þÿ and round the coast had a turbulent discolored appearance ; deep creeks and fissures in the earth are to be seen in several places from some of which water was thrown up, and the smell of sulphur strong in others, as described by one of the Moravian Missionaries who was on his way from Gracehill to his house at Lebanon, and as almost intolerable. The smell was also perceived at Popeshead in a quite opposite direction of the Island. The 11. M. Steamer with the second Januarv Mails arrived at English Harbor direct from England about the time of the Earthquake, but suddenly put about, probably suspecting danger to herself, and proceeded to St. Thomas, without any communication with ttie shore. Since writing the above vve have received authentic intelligence from Montserrat up to yesterday noon. From the New York Commercial Advertiser, January 10, 1813. The Currency Question þÿ In regard to the Exchequer plan, we have sometimes heard a sentiment of this sort expressed: "Let the country suffer till it is willing to come hack, as it must do, to an old fashionable national bank; we want no half way measures " It is well known that we have always expressed our preference for a national bank under proper regulations; but we despair of being able to obtain such an institution in the present state of things. Resides, do people reflect on what is now and what would be the position of the country, if a charter of a national bank were obtained and presented to the public for organization? Do they not perceive that confidence is so prostrated in tnonied corporations, and the resources of the country ate so reduced, that it would lie utterly impossible to gel the stock filled up? Are tlicv not aware that some incipient measures arc requisite to revive confidence, without which a bank charter would remain a dead letter upon the statute hook? It seems to us that the fust step is to regulate exchanges, so as to set business going, to enable different sections of the Union to interchange their produce or transmit it to market, to establish a uniform and fixed system of tates, time and manner, upon which merchants, who are the producers' agents, can fully depend; and thus to divest enterprise of the hazards of speculation, and give it healthy action by moderate a 1 1 reliable profits. This much at least the Exchequer and its branches will accomplish,

and though it will not add any thing to the actual capital ol th-- country, as in fact a national bank would not, it would systematize the action of a portion of what we have and make it useful in <>nr exchanges, while as tilings now are it is wholly idle.

From the St. Thomas Times. MB. ELLIS'S MISSION TO BRAZIL. The special mission of Mr Ellis to Brazil is exciting interest in the City, but the real purpose of his embassy does not appear to be distinctly understood. We believe it to be of a very important nature first, to adjust the term of expiry of the existing commercial treaty with this country; and secondly, to negotiate for a renewal on favourable terms; the slave question and the marriage of the Emperor and his sister being accessories.

THE FIRST ENGLISH TOWN IN CHINA Until within the last year, the probability cfan English town being established in China, and governed by the same, was a thing unheard of. So strongly opposed have the Chinese been to such a measure, and tenacious of strictly adhering to their own customs in all things relating to intercourse with foreign powers, that a fact like this cannot but otherwise than surprise not only themselves but the whole world. That such an event would ever take place has ever been to them held in the light of an impossibility. It is a peculiar feature, that although with English men the Chinese have had greater commercial intercourse than with any other nation, and consequently have received greater benefits from us than from any one or more nations ; there exist greater animosity on their part towards us than any others. This may be traced to the unbending coldness of themselves, and the superior tone of intelligence and authority the English have always maintained. The Chinese cannot and will not hear of a country and its natives being cn an equality with them. The Hong Merchants, men who have had belter opportunities of witnessing that in the arts and sciences, as in things of minor import, England. unquestionably bus the ascendancy, acknowledge our superiority. The Canton Press, of the 12th and 19th February, received by the last overland mails, informs us that great activity prevailed at Hong Kong. Houses and go downs were springing up in all directions, and in a few months, a new and considerable town will

hav - grown into existence. Not only were the government erecting houses and offices for their purposes, but merchants were also gaining more confidence in the perminency of the establishment, while the missionaries of different churches had applied for and obtained grants of land, for the purpose of building chapels and schools. A large native population had already been collected, estimated bv some at 15,000, but chiefly compos'cd of the poorer classes. A magistracy and police had been established, who though, of course, in their infancy, in sullieieuily organised to repress the frequent

thefts and cheating, will, in time be doubtless found efficient The authorities were backward in granting buiiding lots, from the circumstance that the plan for laying out the town was not yet quite completed.

Accounts from Antigua state that the Yellow fever rages fearfully in that Island. Mr. Wood the Provost Marshal has fallen a victim as has also his lady, her mother and one of the children The total absence of the usual trade winds and the most intensely hot, calm weather augurs a very sickly season.

A Daughter's þÿLove. Dear fiiihcr, how i love to gaze upon thee. þÿ Time hath slightly bleached thy locks, thou art the same. Thy kind benignant eye þÿ thy lovely smile, thy noble mien, and bearing, still bespeak thy perfect manhood. Oil how ami enwrapped in thy pure honor þÿ a stain upon thee would wither all the joys that no "» gaily play around my voong and blithe ne heart. 'Tis true 1 have lei t thy home to be another's thro' the joys and perils of a fleeting life but I have not lost my love for thee. When thou didst step within my door, did 1 not clasp thy neck within my hearts embrace and kiss thee then as warmly as when around thy knees 1 used to play at thy own hearth at home. My soul still doats upon my loved and living father. 8ee here, these little buds, fresh from life's great fountain. How they do wind their tender cords of love about our hearts The vine and its branches they like me do claim thee too. Indeed, I do recall what 1 have said before þÿ for 1 do love thee mure than when I quitted home þÿ because oi these near pledges. They are young grafts upon the parent stock, and must live or die beneath its shade. In lime you'll see how they will copy ihee, and in your warm heart you'll find fur them a place just beside the spot, if not the very spot w here thou were wont to keep my own young love.

The livening of Life. þÿ Amid life's varied streams, are sources of transport and pain often mingled and often alternating, we learn at last to prefer those milder and more certain and enduring pleasures which calmly soothes us in the bustle, the labor, and the exe'tement that engage and animate our youth and mature strength. Agitation and emotion at length loose their charm; they disturb more than they amuse its. As age advances to its sober evening, we perceive and appreciate the value of conscious life without pain; of sedate tranquility ; of reposing, yet not inact.ve, thought, of sensibility without perturba. lion of patient hope; of resting moveabiiity ; of sensations that please, but do not agitate; of intellectual ruination: and of those solemn aspirations oi sacred forsight, of prospective gratitude, and of humble reliance on the great mediatorial Benefactor which ciose our mortal days with true dignity, and makes even dissolution an inestimable blessing. þÿ Ibid.

We have good reason to congratulate the community at large, on the comparatively tranquil manner in which the Holidays have been spent this year. I say comparatively" for there is no one who has heretofore witnessed the shameful exhibition ol half dressed girls, reeling through the streets, from the effects of Intoxication, and playing off so many antick tricks, which would puzzle Captain Dick himself to imitate; there in no one I say who ever witnessed all this, will not admit that this year has brought a manifest change for the better. God grant it will continue. þÿ Some may sav, it is the poverty of the times that has caused the change ; but :t is not, although no doubt, it may have contributed to it. There is a spirit of morality abroad ; those who heretofore paraded the streets as objects of laughter and ridicule, are now be IT ginning ? to he actuated bv an honorable spirit of pride, which teaches them that no matter what their colour he, there is nothing pre- to vent them from raising themselves in the scale of society and in the estimation of the good and virtuous þÿ save their own bad conduct. Go on I say young people, as you nave commenced this year ; let us have a still less display of mock Royalty next year. Know that the very persons who would encourage you to acts of dissipation, are the first to point at you with the finger ol scorn, yes! they are the men whom the Sick-House and the Prison may thank for many of her inmates, they are enemies of social order and
happiness.
